utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Today is the 11th of June, 2007. I would like to greet the representatives from the Prosecution, Defence counsel, and the accused, and all the people who are assisting us in the courtroom. I shall first of all give the floor to the registrar who has a few IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you again, Your Honours. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Bo Pellnas. The list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 597. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 598. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 599. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 600. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 601. And finally, the list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit number IC 602, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. We have a witness who is about to come into the courtroom. I believe that this is part of a 92 ter procedure. The Prosecution has given us a set of documents comprising, all in all, 25 documents that have been admitted through this or tendered into evidence through this witness. Three hours and a half have been planned to examine this witness. The Defence teams will have six hours, as we have four days of hearing, and we have shared it out as follows, subject to an agreement between the parties which will be of a different nature. The breakdown would run as follows: 1D one hour, would have one hour; 2D would have one hour; 3D would have 45 minutes; 4D would have one hour and 15 minutes; 5D would have 45 minutes; 6D would have one hour and 15 minutes. So much for the breakdown. This, of course, can be subject to any change or agreement which you would like to reach. The witness will address a number -- the issue of the people he met as part of his activities, members of the 4th Corps. If there are no further issues to be addressed, we shall ask the witness to be brought into the courtroom. I see, Mr. Karnavas, that you've turned to the Bench. Maybe you would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. Mr. President and Your Honours, good afternoon. Good afternoon to everyone. I must say, having read the gentleman's statement very carefully, the one that he gave in 2000, I'm going to be objecting that this statement come in as part of the 92 ter for the following reasons: That if you look at it very carefully, you will see that there are parts in the statement which are nothing more than a compilation of documents that the gentleman purportedly presented to the investigator and then somehow got into the -- into the statement, virtually verbatim, with the sort of -- and if you read the statement, it would appear that the gentleman somehow is commenting on -- on the documents, when in fact all it is is a rewrite of the documents. What's more troublesome to me is, for instance, just as an example, on page 15, on page 15 you see that -- of the statement that he gave on 16 of May 2000, which was also on 9 and 10 June, and it was signed on 10 July 2000, so they met with the gentleman on several occasions, on this page it's a virtual rendition of Exhibit P 00973, the contents of which would appear to be rather legal in a sense, and the gentleman has no legal background other than now being a -- he may have some contact with the legal profession, but I don't see anything in his background at the time, that is, that would enable this gentleman, one, to be able to provide an opinion and to discuss the document as he has in the great detail and to then opine as to what the document meant and for what reasons it was generated. Therefore, there are parts in the statement that I think were nothing more than implants by the Office of the Prosecution, and if you look at the document, it was signed -- his statement was signed on the very last day, 10 July 2000. So it would appear that they met the gentleman on the 16th of May. He may or may not have given him some documents at that point in time. They then return on the 9th and 10 of June where they question him. The OTP then left, drafted a statement, put all sorts of things in it as if it were the gentleman's words, when it was nothing more than a rewrite of certain exhibits, and then had him sign it. Now, I have no objections to the gentleman testifying as to matters for which he's qualified to testify about. I do object, however, to a statement coming in where there -- where the majority of the statement or great portion of the statement is nothing more than documents that he had nothing to do with at the time, and that's my concern. And I raise it at this point in time because the Prosecution may wish to reconsider whether they want to have this witness come in as a 92 ter, because I'm going to be objecting to him going into any of these areas. And I also think it would be advisable, perhaps, to -- before we begin questioning the gentleman on the substance to ask him how this statement was generated. And I leave it to the Bench. I certainly would like to have a crack at it, by way of voir diring the witness before he testifies, that is once he's taken the oath. But I certainly would like to know how this statement was generated, because it appears -- and again, if you just look at -- just as an example and I don't mean to take up too much time, but on page 16, he's talking about laws, and then what caught my fancy is that at one point he says that one particular law is a lex specialis. Now, when you look at the gentleman's background, how would he know that? And then when I look at the document that he makes reference to, it's a verbatim, verbatim, almost word-for-word. The only thing that -- that changes is when they make the introduction as to what is contained in the document, it would appear that the gentleman goes into a narrative, as if these are his words and this is his analysis, when it's nothing more than a rewrite of the documents. Therefore, Your Honours, I strongly object -- I strongly object to the introduction of the documents. I have no problems with the gentleman testifying and his testimony should come in and the Judges should weigh his testimony, but not this particular document and not any of his opinions that are contained within the document unless, unless and I underscore that, some foundation can be laid that the gentleman was knowledgeable about those -- those topics at the time and he's able to comment on them as opposed to presenting documents, and then the Prosecution putting it and bundling it all together, making it look like it's something that came from his particular mouth as a result of having personal experience. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in the courtroom. I support the application that's been made by Mr. Karnavas. I only add this: It seems to me that the Prosecution is trying to get the witness to express a legal opinion which he's not only unqualified to give but they're doing it, of course, without observing the proper formalities for an expert witness under Rule 94 bis, and for those reasons, Your Honour, there are certain parts of the witness's statement that may be admissible. Clearly other parts are not. And it would be really counter-productive to proceed with this witness as a 92 ter witness when we may have to choose between different parts of the statement. So for that reason, Your Honour, I would support what Mr. Karnavas has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The Petkovic Defence also supports what our learned friends have said. The more one looks into the statement, the more one sees that quite substantial passages are subject to exactly the vice that our learned friends indicate. It appears in some cases, for example, that a document, because it happens to pass through this gentleman's hands as a translator, then becomes a document on which he then expresses some expert or quasi-expert view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Ms. Gillett or Mr. Scott, would you like to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, good afternoon to you, Mr. President, Your Honours, and everyone in the courtroom. Your Honour, I think much too much is being made of this. What appears to have been the case is it's not -- it's not the first time I've seen this happen, is that sometimes when there is a lengthy interview and the investigator goes into the field and there are a number of documents that are involved, what apparently happened is a lot of the documents, rather than quote extensively from the documents, a lot of documents were essentially incorporated into the statement. I don't think there's any big mystery or secret about that. It would be -- apparently the difference would be, apparently, that if all the documents could be attached to the statement and if he could be asked to essentially go through and read the statement, go through and read each document and then make comment or in this case, the investigator in 2000, some years -- some many years ago prepared it in the way that he or she did. I don't think there's anything sinister in it. If on an individual item basis there is something that counsel says, for instance, is a legal opinion then I think we can deal with that as an individual issue. I can respond further to any suggestion, unfortunate as they may be, that this -- there is some sinister motive or trickery involved here to get some evidence in that the Prosecution wouldn't think it could otherwise get in. Frankly, it never even occurred to us. It was simply a lengthy witness with a number of statements that we thought would be most efficiently taken in this way. All the documents that are referenced or the vast majority of them are exhibits. They would be put to the witness in any event. So quite frankly, I think this is a mountain out of a molehill. The preparation has been done on the basis of -- that is a -- the preparation has been done on the basis that it will be taken as a 92 ter and the time estimate was done accordingly. If the Chamber changes its view, decides to take the witness as a viva voce witness, then additional preparation will be required and the time estimate will have to be changed. This was announced last week, and it's unfortunate that it's raised -- these comments are made just immediately previous to the witness coming into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I reassure Mr. Scott that certainly there wasn't a suggestion of sinister motive or trickery --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, there were by some.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott, it's a very good practice in this courtroom, I think, if one of us stands up as time and one of us speaks at a time, as I allowed you to do a moment ago. I absolutely do not make and did not make any such suggestion, but what is, and the phrase I would use, what is sleight of hand - it may be forensic sleight of hand - is to try, in some way, to convert the issue between us into a question, has there been trickery, has there been a sinister motive. That's not the point. It's -- the question is whether evidence is properly admissible or not, not whether there's been some sinister motive or trickery which we do not assert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, for interrupting Mr. Stewart. My apology to him. My point is this: Unfortunately, what so often happens is a number of Defence counsel get up, some of them state different positions, and the Prosecution, of course, responds and I suppose sometimes generic, too generically. Perhaps I should identify individual counsel. I don't think Mr. Stewart suggested that. I think there was some suggestion to some degree by both Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Murphy that the Prosecution was attempting to get evidence in, in some way that otherwise would not be able to. So I stand corrected by Mr. Stewart but my comments stand in general. Your Honour, first there's no basis --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm being interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right, I accept that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is -- this is a mountain out of a molehill. This is a statement of the witness. Yes, documents have been incorporated in some instances into the text of the statement. The Court -- the Chamber can well distinguish that, if need be. This is really -- this is really -- this is really a nothing issue, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, I would just like to say though that what Mr. Scott just said, "I don't think Mr. Stewart suggested that. I think there was some suggestion by some degree by both Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Murphy that the Prosecution was attempting to get evidence in that it otherwise would not be able to do so." That suggestion I do make. I don't make a suggestion of sinister motive or trickery. One needs to be very precise about what is being said. I do associate myself with my learned friends about that. I'm not sure that my learned friends made any allegations of sinister motive or trickery. I certainly didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My objections, Your Honour, is that the statement should be of the -- of his own making. It should be his statement. It is not his statement. What it is is the Prosecution has met with the gentleman, then they went back and they put it together and they inserted certain documents into the statement, and now they have the gentleman sign it as if this was his statement. That's what I object to. Now, I'm not suggesting that they can't get those documents in. I am saying that certain documents, this particular witness is not competent to testify about, and so because the gentleman hands the documents over doesn't necessarily mean that he's competent to testify, and putting that into the statement itself gives the appearance, rightly or wrongly, that the gentleman is capable of testifying about the contents of the documents and that's why I raised it. So they may wish to switch and just take viva voce testimony and the documents can be introduced, and then we can fight out what he can and cannot testify with respect to certain documents. But if he's not competent, he's not competent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, all the documents are listed -- excuse me. All the documents are known. I suggest this is no different than any other witness. The counsel can question any individual document, put it to the witness during cross-examination, and just like any other witness that we deal with, if they put it to the witness and if they feel that they can lay a foundation through the witness that the document shouldn't be admitted to the witness, then of course they can file their objections at the end of the examination. But again this is just -- this is -- this is not a significant complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just spent 20 minutes discussing this. Mr. Karnavas -- while Mr. Karnavas was speaking, I looked at the written document, and I acknowledge as follows: The witness was heard by Mr. Spork on the 16th of May in the year 2000. After that a few weeks later, on the 10th of June 2000, and then a month later on the 10th of July, 2000. On the 10th of July, 2000, the person in signed the statement, which is the 27-page statement, and he indicated that it had been read out to him in his own language. In the 26-page statement, we can see that 13 documents are mentioned. The latter are referenced in his statement. And the written statement is clearly based on these documents. After that, the documents are to be found on page 25. We have a report which is dated the 9th of March, 1994, and point 2, we have a copy of the president of Mostar, who is sending a letter. So these 13 documents can be found in his written statement. After that the witness is heard again on the 18th of January, 2004. Not by Mr. Spork this time but by Ms. Egels, assisted by Susan Tucker, and in his statement, which is a few pages long, he addresses some of these issues which had already been addressed in the previous written statement. And a while ago on the 15th of May, 2007, he's heard again by Mr. Spork and in his 15th of May, 2007 statement several documents are again mentioned. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 documents are mentioned. All these documents are seemingly included in the binders in front us. As far as I'm concerned, it seems that most of the statements are based on the documents. Let remind you of Rule 92 ter (A)(iii). Let me read it out to you. "The witness testifies that the written statement or the statement taken during the interview replicates his -- what he has said and he would see -- he would say the same if he were to be asked the question again." Even if the investigator has drafted a the statement, the witness has re-read the statement, has authenticated it, and has signed it, and has acknowledged it as truthful. This is how we stand. The legal officer has just told me that we had the same problem with Witness B1 when this procedure had been triggered. I think my colleague on the -- my left-hand side wishes to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not without understanding for the objections of the Defence, because there are rules for the admission of documents, and if documents are read to a witness and then appear in the transcript, that, a little bit, gives the impression of sneaking them into our documentation. Also, I think that there is a certain insecurity on how the witness was brought to make the commenting declarations he made, but I think that can easily be done here. Mr. Karnavas has already pointed out he can be asked whether these were his comments or whether they were suggested to him. There's also the possibility of cross-examination. Mainly the documents, I think, will anyway be presented in the original by the OTP, and I think it was useful to -- having drawn our attention to this, and we will be very careful about it and are prepared certainly to have what the witness will say today be decisive and not what is in the statement. I think -- can the Defence live with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Precisely. That's what exactly -- I wanted to highlight and I wanted to be fair to the Prosecutor that I was going to raise certain objections to the form of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I think that His Honour has hit the nail right on the head. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And can the Prosecution live with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't think -- as far as I know, and it's actually Ms. Gillett's witness and I apologise for intervening. As far as I know, all the exhibits that will be put to the witness are in the bundle. They will be individually addressed by the witness. If the Chamber finds at the end of the day it feels that there are some documents that's quoted or referred to in the body of the statement that the Chamber is uncomfortable with, we can certainly address that. It may not be the best way to take a statement but that's the way the statement was taken in 2000, some seven years ago. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you -- usher, could you bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the quote from Rule 92 ter: "The witness attests that the written statement or transcript accurately reflects that witness' declaration and what the witness would say if examined."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Let me make sure you understand the translation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like you to stand so that you can take the solemn declaration. For the purpose of the transcript, could you give me your first name, family name and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zlatan Buljko. I was born on the 19th of July, 1954, in Gorazde, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At present, I'm working as a consultant on a project to reform the local government in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you already testified before an International Tribunal or a national court about events that unfolded in your country, or is it the first time you come to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before an international court, the first time, but I testified in Mostar, in the case of Romeo Blazevic, with respect to my expulsion on the 9th of May, 1993. That is the only case which relates to the situation that took place in western -- in Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the case you have just mentioned, which was tried before the tribunal in Mostar, was this a criminal procedure or civil procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was a criminal procedure. I'm not quite sure, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Romeo Blazevic, was he convicted or wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he was not convicted. I think that the proceedings are either still ongoing, or that the outcome was positive as far as he was concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you testify before a Bench or before an investigating judge? Let me repeat my question. When you testified before the tribunal in Mostar, were there judges, a prosecutor, and attorneys and Mr. Blazevic, or did you investigate before an investigating judge, when there was only one judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the first case; before a judge, a prosecutor, attorneys, and the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like you to read the text of the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit. So first let me give you some explanations regarding the four days of hearing that have been set aside regarding your testimony. You might be surprised by the difference between this proceeding and what happened in Mostar. In -- for this proceed -- proceeding, you'll first answer questions that will put to you by the representative of the Prosecution which I'm sure you've met. She will ask you a number of questions and she will also show you a number of documents. And after that phase, which will take some time, counsel for Defence, which are on your left, and you see that there's a great number of them, and possibly the accused, will start asking questions in turn. It will be the cross-examination phase. The three Judges on the Bench can ask a question to you at any time during the procedure. However, we'd rather now wait for all questions during the examination phase and the cross-examination phase be over before we actually put questions, unless there's a document that's been presented, because if there's a document being presented on screen, we'd rather ask the questions right away in order to make sure that we don't disturb the proceedings. So please try and be extremely specific in the answers you give. If you don't understand a question, don't hesitate to ask for a reformulation of the question. There will be a break every hour and a half. These are 20-minute breaks. If at any time you feel ill or you feel uncomfortable for any reason, please say so and we can immediately stop the proceedings. So this is how the hearing is going to be held. If you have a question to put to a Judge, you can do so. I will now give the floor to Prosecution for this 92 ter procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: As Your Honour already knows, this witness is being called pursuant to the procedure under Rule 92 ter, and as has become the practice in this court, a summary of that witness's evidence is read into the record purely as a matter of the public record, before I commence the admission of the statement procedure and then go on to ask the further questions. For the benefit of the Court, this summary is entirely based on the Rule 65 ter description that was submitted by the Prosecution along with this witness. It is a little bit of a lengthy summary as one might expect, given that this witness has provided one very lengthy statement and two other somewhat shorter statements. The summary commences as follows: The witness gives information about the political background in the Mostar region from 1990 onwards; The creation of the HZ HB in 1991; the establishment of the HOS and the HVO; the hand-over of power by the SDA to the HDZ in Mostar in 1992 and the consequences thereof; the takeover by the HVO of the civilian police structures in Mostar and the consequences thereof in 1993; the various laws passed by the HZ HB HVO in order to short-circuit the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In June 1992, the witness, together with other Bosnian Muslim employees, was fired from his job at a Mostar company that only kept Bosnian Croats employed. In April 1993, the witness became the interpreter for Arif Pasalic, commander of the ABiH 4th Corps, and he attended most of the negotiations between the HVO, the ABiH, and the international organisations in the Mostar area between April and the end of June of 1993. He confirms that during that time, Berislav Pusic was part of most of these meetings. He gives information about the breakout of the conflict between HVO and ABiH in Mostar in April 1993. On the 9th of May, 1993, the witness was evicted from his apartment by HVO soldiers after having to hand over all valuables. He was expelled together with other Bosnian Muslim neighbours to East Mostar. That day he also witnessed the shelling of East Mostar and heard the speech given by Jadran Topic on the radio. On the 12th of May, 1993, the witness was part of a negotiation meeting where Milivoj Petkovic was representing the HVO and signed an agreement on the cessation of hostilities. He explains the content of that agreement and its improper implementation. The witness gives information about other agreements between the HVO and the ABiH that were not respected, such as the 19th of May, 1993 agreement on the UN civil police monitors, and the 25th of May, 1993, and 8th of June, 1993, agreements on the realisation of the agreement about the cessation of hostilities. At the end of June 1993, the witness was appointed by General Arif Pasalic to re-establish civilian authorities and institutions in East Mostar and to coordinate humanitarian activities. The witness describes the process, started by the East Mostar War Presidency, attempting to list the Bosnian Muslim prisoners held in HVO detention centres. He explains that such lists were handed over to the HVO during negotiation meetings and more specifically to Berislav Pusic. On the 24th of August, 1993, he was part of the ABiH team that negotiated with the HVO the entrance of the first humanitarian convoy into East Mostar. He gives information about the involvement of Bruno Stojic in these negotiations and the content of the negotiations, as well as the agreement reached. The witness describes the difficulties linked to the access of humanitarian -- access of humanitarian aid to East Mostar due to the blockade by the HVO. He also describes the unbearable living conditions for civilians in East Mostar. The witness describes medical evacuations from East Mostar in September and November 1993, and the HVO shelling of the East Mostar war hospital. In September 1993, the witness was appointed head of the office for displaced persons and refugees for the Herzegovina area by the president of the Mostar War Presidency. He gives detailed information about the high influx of displaced and expelled Muslims into East Mostar and reports about the ethnic cleansing of the municipalities of Mostar, Stolac, Capljina, Ljubuski by the HVO since April 1993. He explains how he heard on numerous occasions that Bosnian Muslims were either expelled to ABiH-controlled territory or to third countries by the HVO. He gives information about the involvement of the Republic of Croatia in these deportations. That ends the 65 ter description of the evidence contained in the witness's statements, the three of them. I'll now commence the admission of the statement procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buljko. Mr. Buljko, do you remember being interviewed on several occasions by the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recall that that was on the 16th of May, the 9th and 10th of June and the 10th of July in 2000?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And then again on the 18th of January 2004?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And lastly, on the 15th of May, 2007?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: On each of those occasions did you answer the questions that were asked of you truthfully?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes, my answers were truthful.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did you also do so voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, at the end of the interview process in 2000, on the 10th of July, also in 2004, on the 18th of January, 2004, and the 15th of May, 2007, do you recall the statements being read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you also recall signing each of the statements on each of those occasions, confirming that they were true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes. I signed them and I initialed each and every page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could a hard copy of each of the three statements that are Exhibits 10069, 10070 and 10071 be placed in front of the Witness? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, have you had the opportunity to re-read these statements prior to coming into court?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, by looking at the statements in front of you, and I believe it's the English versions of the statements, are you able to confirm that those are your initials on each of the pages of the English version of all three statements?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes. These are my initials.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And is your signature on the last page of the statement, all three of the statements?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: If I were to ask you questions today about the subject matters contained in these written statements, would your answers be reflected by the contents of those statements?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They are a reflection of that, but they require some additional explanations too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Buljko, having re-read these statements in your own language, I believe you mentioned there was one correction at least that you wanted to make, and that was on page 3 of the English -- sorry, page 20 of the B/C/S version of the 2000 statement and page 13 of the English version. It was a matter of translation. Are you able to find those two pages, page 13 of the English and page 20 of the B/C/S, and explain what it is you wanted to correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Let me just find it. The structure of the sentence wasn't right, so I had an objection. I cannot find my way here. Is it really page 20?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: It's page 20 of the B/C/S version, and it's halfway down the page. The paragraph just above where it says "Vladislav Pogarcic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps the Madam Prosecutor can lead the witness since they've already had this conversation. So there's no sense in going through this kabuki dance. Just read it to him and we can go through it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'll do my best to lead the witness. Actually in B/C/S, and so as far as sentence structure is concerned, I'm somewhat lost but it was the English version I understand, you are in agreement, Mr. Buljko, with the English version that reads, "because it took till 1994 before all needed International Organisations were able to actually start their aid programs in East Mostar." But in the B/C/S version, I believe you had a correction after it reads, "zato sto sve potrebne medjunarodne organizacije", you wish to correct to read --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I found it. I have found it. Just a moment, please. What it says here the international organisations were able to monitor the situation in East Mostar because it took till 1994, yes, because international organisations were -- before all needed international organisations were able to actually start their aid programmes in East Mostar, till 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour perhaps the gentleman, since he supposedly speaks English and was a translator and obviously would know English grammar, I would suspect, perhaps he could just tell us in English how it should be corrected in the English, since the Court is going to be dealing with the English and not the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: This is the problem, Your Honour. The witness's correction was not in the English. He was happy with the English version. He was concerned that the B/C/S version sentence structure reflected the English structure correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And so it's almost impossible for us to understand in English the correction. It's a matter of sentence structure in the B/C/S and I have to respect that the witness wished to make this correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please -- yes, Witness. In the B/C/S text, which is a translation from the English, what's the problem? Could you tell us exactly what you want corrected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This second part of the sentence towards the end of the paragraph, it should say because all the way up to 1994, up to 1994, this period had to elapse before all necessary international organisations were in a position actually to start their own programmes of aid in Mostar, in East Mostar. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think this -- this is a bit Platonic, Witness, because we are working in English; the transcript is in English. The judgement will be in French, but we'll only read English as a basis for it. So I -- with all respect, and I highly respect your wish to have precision all around, if the English version is okay with you, I think the rest is a bit an excess of perfectionism. Thank you anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but unless the B/C/S version did not say the same thing as the English version. Some of our accused do not understand English, and they're fully entitled to understand in their own language what the document actually states. So on this point, could you tell us exactly what the difference was in the original B/C/S version and the new B/C/S version that you have just told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the English version, it is quite accurate. What needs to be adjusted is the translation from English into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I be of assistance? Can we ask the witness to read out for us what it is that he wrote in English and then our interpreters will interpret that and then we will understand what he's trying to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what is the page in B/C/S, in the B/C/S version? Could you tell us exactly what is the page and what is the paragraph involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 20. The paragraph is one, two, three, four; it's the fourth paragraph. The first sentence -- the first sentence is all right. So it's the second sentence. It was: "It became obvious that he was not supportive of the idea that the international organisations were able to monitor the situation in East Mostar." That's all right. "Because it took till 1994," that is to say that that period had to elapse, "before all needed international organisations were able to actually start their aid programmes in East Mostar." That's it. That is my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Ms. Nozica's satisfied. I think we can pursue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Witness, having --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She's not satisfied. She's up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not a question of my satisfaction, but at least, I have understood, I think, what the witness is trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood also. Ms. Gillett, you have the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, having made that correction, do you stand by the contents of these three statements as being true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, staying with the statement of 10th of July, 2000, your first statement, effectively, if I can call it that way, you mention at page 3 of the 2000 statement that because of the threat of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Bosnian Croats established, for defence purposes, their own HOS forces, commanded by a Bosnian Croat named Blaz Kraljevic. When was this H-O-S, HOS, established?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: The armed section of the HOS was established sometime in the beginning of 1991, and there were three stages involved. The first stage was that they had their armed forces that were independent. Then they coordinated with the HVO and then they were completely subordinated to the HVO after the killing of Blaz Kraljevic on the 12th of August 1992 in the hamlet of Glamuzine near Krusevo. Then on the 28th of August it was subordinated when Mr. Ante Prkacin and Mr. Mate Boban signed this subordination to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Moving on to page 4 of the English version of your statement and page 6 of the B/C/S version, the paragraph that relates to a temporary agreement between the SDA and HDZ whereby the SDA transferred all political power in the Mostar municipality to the HDZ. At that time, do you know who was in charge of the HDZ and who was in charge of the HVO, that time being, as you mention in your statement, the 27th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: As for the HDZ, after Milivoj Gagro, as far as I can remember it was Mr. Bruno Stojic. And after him in Mostar, it was Jadranko Topic. As for the SDA as I've already stated here, Ismet Hadziosmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: So on the 27th of April, 1992, the date mentioned in your statement who was in charge of the HDZ after the three persons that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, in that same paragraph, this agreement, you mention this agreement was the HDZ HVO was allowed to make all military decisions in relation to the defence of Mostar. Do you know who was responsible for making such decisions?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: In view of the fact that cooperation between the SDA and the HDZ went on for a while, was not interrupted, as for the HDZ in Mostar, well, again I'm saying I think it's Mr. Stojic. In that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you also know by what process those decisions were taken?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I cannot say much about that because I was not involved in such processes. Decision-making processes, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, in relation to your job at Apro, A-p-r-o,, you were fired on the 25th of June, 1992, as mentioned at page 5 of the English version of your statement and page 6 of the B/C/S version, and you say you believe that this was because you are Muslim, as there were no Bosnian Croats that were fired, although that was not the official reason given to you. Now, out of the total of 28 employees that you say worked there, how many of these employees were actually retained?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Ten were retained. Out of the ten employees, two were Bosnian Muslims who were retained. Well, one person was kept on account of bookkeeping, and there was this other person who was kept there because we did quite a bit of work there with imported goods, and we had duty-free shops, and in storerooms there were a lot of products left, and this Bosnian Muslim was in charge of the inventories. I think that is the reason why they were retained, in order to know what the financial situation in the company was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Why do you believe that you were fired because you were a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't only me that was fired. My colleagues, the Serbs, had already left Mostar, so that left the Croats and the Muslims. However, in the work that I was doing, or rather the reason I was given was for economic reasons. That's why they said I was let go. But if you knew the situation in Mostar during those days and later on, I know that the majority of Bosnian Muslims lost their jobs and that they were not able to find employment. Some of them did stay on, but a very small number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Turning to the bottom of page 6 of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Witness, please. I have a question about something. You seem to be a rather learned man. You have been to university. You speak French, English, Italian, and Russian, and you are conversant in a number of foreign languages. On looking at your answers, you seem to fully understand the questions that are being put to you. So I would like to get back to the question of the time you were fired. On page 3 of the English version, you mention that you were not really told why you were fired, and you were told that you were fired for economic reasons. You must have had a contract nonetheless, and in your country contracts are governed by law, and if you are fired without no reason whatsoever, can you not turn to the law and seize the judge in charge of those matters? It would be, of course, part of labour law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the situation in Mostar and the fact that the law was not respected and that institutions of that kind did not exist, I don't know who I could contact. I know what my rights were, but we had contracts which were not short-term contracts, one, two, three years, as they are today. We had contracts for an unspecified period of time which provided us with a certain amount of security. They meant that we could earn our living and that we were secure in our jobs, but at that point there was nobody that I could contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were fired in 1992. Everything collapsed. Were there no judges? Was nothing working any more? What was the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be more or less the case. For questions of that kind there was what we called courts of associated labour. So the system was quite different at the time. But in Mostar after the events that took place during that period of time and after the Serb forces had withdrawn, the situation was chaotic, to be quite frank. So that I really don't know who I could have contacted at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to be of some assistance to the Trial Chamber. On page 1 he indicates that at that point in time he was a sales manager, and I guess he was engaged in import/export. In line with your questions, perhaps you should ask the gentleman whether he was able to carry out his functions at that period of time, and of course, you know, it might also be relevant whether he was there the entire time, from the time that the Serb aggression began or whether he was absent and not around, and therefore perhaps that might also have been one of the reasons. In other words, one, the company wasn't functioning, due to his particular position; and two, he had been absent because he was out of the country for two months, and perhaps whether he raised that with any labour union or labour court or what have you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, as far as the reasons are concerned, the reasons why you were fired, according to Defence counsel you were working for a company that was involved in import and export. Given the situation at the time and that the Serbs had withdrawn and the war was on, maybe the -- this company was not operating as it should and you were not there yourself. What can you say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the company could have continued operating because it had enough food supplies and goods supplies which it sold in its retail shops. So the possibility did exist for economic activities to be continued. Now, it was true that I was absent for a certain amount of time. However, the director who was there before the gentleman I mention in my statement authorised me to go and take my family to safety. I had a small child, and my child was just one year old, and I had to take my family out of the chaos that reigned in Mostar. And he said that I could come back whenever I wished. I did come back, but he was replaced. Now, on the basis of the agreement of the 27th of April that I mention between the SDA and the HDZ he personally told me, he said to me, "Zlatan, I'm not the director here any more. I don't know what's going to happen in the future." And when Mr. Bracic whom I also mention as being somebody -- as the man who took over, that is to say who received authorisation from the HDZ to be the director, he then began to implement his own policy, probably the policy that was imposed upon him, and the result of that was that I was dismissed. Not only me but my other colleagues too. I was told that I don't have to come to work any more. So I think I've made myself quite clear. As I said, I was authorised to take my family out of Mostar as thousands of other Mostar families did at the time, and I state that in my statement, and I was authorised to return because I thought my job would be waiting for me when I came back. However, that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, moving to the bottom of page 6 of the B/C/S version of your statement, and it's about halfway down page 5 of the English version, you state that the HVO stopped supplying the ABiH. What did the HVO stop supplying the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: When I joined the BH army -- or, actually, that followed. My joining up followed after the food supplies and medical supplies came into ABiH. That is to say, in July, a logistical unit was formed of the Independent Mostar Brigade as it was called at the time, and later became known as the Mostar Brigade, and afterwards the 41st famous -- famed Mostar Brigade. Now, my friends, most of them didn't have jobs either. They informed me that they needed somebody to help them out who had experience with commercial jobs in order to set up a logistical unit for the supply -- food -- for food supplies and medical supplies. And so around the 23rd of August, I joined the Mostar Brigade and was a member of the logistics of the Mostar Brigade. And the condition for that was -- or the reason for that was because food and medicines had stopped coming in, had stopped being sent in by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you know who took the decision to stop the supply of the food and medicines coming in?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: At the time I was not in the BH army. All I know is that my friends told me that that was the reason. But they didn't give me the names of the people who were in charge of things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know on what level such decision was taken, whether it was on a local level or it was on a larger level than that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I think it was at a local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this was pure speculation. The witness started off by saying that he didn't know where the decision was made and then he was asked again at local or a higher level, and then he said he thought it was a local level. That is speculation. Or perhaps he should be asked on what grounds, since he's already given his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I be allowed to reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kindly answer the question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked -- the first question was who the people were involved. I said I did not know, that I wasn't told. Then the second question was the following: I was asked at what level, was it at the level of Mostar or was it further afield. I said it was the local level, which means at the level of Mostar. So I think these were two separate questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's not the issue whether they were two separate questions. Obviously there were two separate questions. But if he didn't know the first one, he is called to speculate on the second one, or at least --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- his answer is speculative at best. Now, if he can demonstrate exactly how he knows, with a document, a name, a date, a place, something, fine, otherwise I think we get the point. It's speculative.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps if I could be permitted to ask my follow-up question which was to ask why the witness thinks it was on the local level, in order that it maybe put to rest whether or not it is purely speculative or if there is some basis for the witness saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But asking him to think. "Does he know," that's the predicate. Does he know for a fact. If he doesn't know, then I think anything other than that calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that a decision was taken at a particular level. Are you speculating, or do you know at what level such a decision was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It did not happen in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina as it did in Mostar. I know everything was okay in Sarajevo and Tuzla, but this is what happened in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's no answer. The witness did not answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you answer the Prosecutor's question, when you say at what level the decision was taken, what enables you to say this with a degree of certainty or not? Is it that you have knowledge of this? Do you know who the decision-makers were, or are you just assuming this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no knowledge as to who made the decision. I said earlier on that I was called upon to join the Independent Mostar Brigade, that I was told a logistic unit was being set up because the HVO had stopped sending supplies of food and medicines to the international -- Independent Mostar Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, in your capacity as member of the logistical unit of the ABiH, officially becoming a member as you did on the 23rd of August, 1992, what did you wear in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I mostly wore civilian clothing since there weren't enough uniforms to go around. The uniforms were issued to soldiers first of all, those who were up at the front lines. And the logistical unit received uniforms, I think it was in the spring of 1993, and that's when I was issued a uniform, too, but I only wore it to attend meetings of our logistical unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Still on page 5 of the English version of the statement, but page 7 of the B/C/S version, you state that you went to Zagreb to try to get financial resources for the ABiH salaries. Why did you go to Zagreb to do this?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: The electrical industry of Bosnia-Herzegovina was issued something authorised by the BH government, and according to this agreement the electrical industry of Bosnia-Herzegovina was to abide by the agreement that was signed between the electrical industry and the government with respect to financial resources, but the electrical industry of Croatia never signed the agreement and the money was never paid out as had been agreed. Now, the reason for that was that the Republic of Croatia bought electricity. It still needs to buy electricity and there are certain agreements that need to be respected which involve payment, payment for electricity used.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What was the connection to the payment of the ABiH salaries?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: It was a decision taken by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is a complicated question. I would like to sum it up for you, and correct me if I'm wrong. According to what you've told us, the Republic of Croatia buys electricity from the company Elektroprivreda. From what I understood, there are certain -- there are bonds that are issued, but the ABiH soldiers need to be paid, and Sarajevo and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina has told the ABiH that to get paid, the Republic of Croatia needed to redeem the bonds. In other words, the bonds needed to be redeemed in order to get electricity. This is rather complicated, but from what you've said I think this is what I understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the BH army were not paid, and in my statement I said that many Bosnian Muslims joined the HVO for two reasons. One, because it was better equipped; and second, because they received regular salaries. But the members of the BH army did not. So during that period of time covering several months these costs had to be covered, and how this was to be done was on the basis of this decision and these bonds. I know it's a complex question and has to do with the situation of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know who it was on behalf of the BH army, but I see that for the Elektroprivreda or electrical industry of Bosnia-Herzegovina it was the director who signed the agreement, and at that time the director of the Croatian electrical industry or Elektroprivreda Hrvatska was supposed to sign.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, bottom of page 5 of the English version of the statement and the top of page 8 of the B/C/S version of your statement, still with the 2000 statement. You talk about working as an interpreter for Arif Pasalic and attending most of the negotiation meetings between ABiH and HVO and international organisations in the Mostar area. What was the extent of your role at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I was always invited by Mr. Arif Pasalic or others, other participants in the negotiations, to help them if the need arose. As many international institutions and UN organisations, UNPROFOR and so on and so forth, ECMM, took part. They attended these meetings. So I was called upon to assist, and I would go when invited. Later on, I went to represent the civilian authorities and the civilian police as well and representatives of the international community. But in this case, he asked me to go because he knew I spoke foreign languages. And he trusted me when it came to the translation and interpretation. He knew that it would be done properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're not very accurate. A Judge would like to understand what part you played. I have the feeling that you played two parts. A, you were an interpreter because you are conversant in foreign languages, in English certainly, and you then translate for Mr. Pasalic or the ABiH representatives. It seems to me, according to what you said, that there's a second part that you play. On line 25 of page 35, you say that you represent the civil authorities, and you quote, as an example, the police, for instance. So you can't be an interpreter or negotiator all in one. Were you deemed both at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I interpreted for the needs of the civilian police when they had negotiations with UN CIVPOL or with the military observers from the United Nations. So I wasn't only interpreting for Mr. Pasalic but for other institutions as well -- or, rather, for all the institutions in Eastern Mostar at the time. My role later on -- well, I was invited to attend the meetings and to interpret, but I of course did other work as well, and this is what I want to tell you. Since I was a member of the 41st famed Motorised Brigade, whose commander was the late Midhad Hujdur, nicknamed Hujka, who was killed, Mr. Pasalic asked for authorisation from my commander, that is to say, from Mr. Midhad Hujdur, nicknamed Hujka, to go and allow me to attend these meeting with him and to interpret for him. So I had to obey and comply. And the negotiations that we mentioned a moment ago, at those negotiations I was the interpreter, and I interpreted for most of the negotiations conducted in Mostar at that period. And I would like to emphasise the following the negotiations didn't last all day every day, so I worked as much as they needed me. I would go with the representatives of the BH army or the commission for prisoner exchange and so on and so forth, and then I would go back to my own job and carry on doing that when I didn't need to interpret, and I told you what that other job was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was a very precise question, and you don't answer it in a precise manner. During the negotiations did you have full powers to negotiate? According to the answer you gave us, you seem to be saying that you were there to play the part of an interpreter, but as far as the 41st Brigade is concerned, there must have been an officer there who was representing the 41st Brigade. You were not the 41st Brigade representative during these negotiations, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I wasn't a representative of the brigade. I was just the interpreter at the negotiations, and I did not have any military authorisation or competence to negotiate. So as we say, I was in the rear, as are all interpreters, in the background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, at least that is an accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, at these meetings that you attended whereby international organisations, ABiH and HVO, were participating in the Mostar area, who would attend to represent the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: The negotiations, well, Mr. Arif Pasalic, Suad Cupina, Mr. Alija Alikadic later on, Mr. Dziho. Those were the individuals who conducted the negotiations on behalf of the BH army. But depending on the topic under discussion, there were other people, too, and they held certain positions in the army or in the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Those people you've mentioned, in terms of their hierarchy what was their authority or ability to take decisions at the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: As far as I know, on behalf of the BH army the decisions were taken by -- or, rather, the decisions that were made at these meetings prevailed. The representatives representing the army or the civilian authorities were able to make decisions during the negotiations, except under certain circumstances where they had to refer back to some other authority, consult some other authority. If it was at the commission for prisoner exchange, for example, or the exchange of the bodies of persons who had been killed, they had to consult the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Equally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett, we're going to have a break now because it's a quarter to 4.00, and we shall have a 20-minute break and resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Prosecution can resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, just before the break I'd asked you about who would attend as a representative from the ABiH and a few further questions from that. The question I now ask you is in relation to those meetings that you attended, who would attend as a representative from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Slavko Puljic, Tihomir Maric were there on behalf of the HVO, then Mr. Pusic attended most of these meetings as far as I can remember. That would be about it for the period when I was present at the negotiations. .

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And, again, as I asked you in relation to the ABiH, as far as the HVO is concerned, out of the persons that you just mentioned who represented the HVO at these meetings, in terms of their hierarchy what authority did they have to take decisions during those negotiations, during those meetings that you attended?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Unless a foundation is laid, it's speculative. She needs to lay a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you very much. If we are still talking about the 2000 statement as we are, I think, then this would be something new because it didn't really exist in the statement, the question of authority, responsibilities, powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett. Ms. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, you've mentioned three persons, I think it was, who attended the meetings as representatives of the HVO. What positions did they hold?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: They had military and civilian positions. However, I think that they could not make any decisions at these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, Ms. Gillett should have asked a question and she's not asking it, so I will put to you. When you had these meetings ABiH and HVO, were they sitting around a table and you as an interpreter you were next to them or behind them? Can you tell us exactly how it was organised? Was it extremely formal? Did you have an agenda? Was anyone chairing the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part the meetings were chaired by representatives of the international community, whereas the delegations of the armija and the HVO sat on their respective sides. So these were formal meetings. I sat near the representative of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or a representative who would be conducting the negotiations. In the period after that, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So were you sitting next to them or behind them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, at the meetings that you attended at which Mr. Pusic also attended, what position did Mr. Pusic hold at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Mr. Pusic was then the representative of the civilian authorities, if I understood things correctly. However, as far as I know, he was a member of the negotiating team. I don't know what his exact position was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know whether his position was a high or a low or a middling ranking position?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: A low position, I think, a low-ranking position.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know what authority Mr. Pusic had to make any decisions at the meetings you attended?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Pusic could not make any decisions at the meetings. He could, for example, collect lists of prisoners, wounded persons, and so on, but specifically at meetings he could not make any decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: At those meetings that you attended, do you know who on the HVO side made the decisions?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: In my assessment these would have to be higher structures of the HVO or the HDZ at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we know what an international meeting is like. There will be the international representative, and then on both sides of the table you will have the HVO on one side and the ABiH on the other side. The international representative is chairing and will open the meeting, and of course will give the floor to HVO and to the ABiH, and normally in this kind of meeting the one taking the floor is the higher level, you know. It's not the lower-level person that's going to take the floor. So in this configuration, would Mr. Pusic speak first, or would he take the floor after other HVO members have spoken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said who the main representatives were in that period at the negotiations. Mr. Pusic spoke very little. He would always speak later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it wasn't him who was taking the decisions for the HVO. It was the other HVO representatives that would be making the decisions. Earlier you gave us names of HVO members. Could you state them again, those who were also present in addition to Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said Slavko Puljic, and Tihomir Maric in the period that we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: At the meetings that you attended when Mr. Pusic was present, who else apart from Mr. Pusic would be present from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: At the initial meetings, that is to say, after the 9th of May when the conflict broke out, at the negotiations I saw Mr. Petkovic. I would see Jadranko Topic as well, who during the first negotiations we had in this building that is in the street of Ante Zujanica, he threw out of the entire negotiating team of the international community, of the BH army, of the HVO, everybody. Then some other persons appeared who had some different kind of authority, but I cannot recall exactly what that was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: From your attendance at these meetings, do -- do you know which of the HVO representatives present at the meeting was taking the decisions that were made?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to intervene at this point. The witness has testified that he was present at these meetings as an interpreter on behalf of the ABiH side. How can it possibly be appropriate to ask him about the inner workings of the HVO negotiating team? Your Honour, this is not the right witness for these questions, and I object to this whole line of questioning as calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. But what I'm interested in is how it all worked. So for example, when there was a topic X that was to be discussed, there were discussions between the two sides. And when finishing the meeting on this topic, I guess that the representative of the international community would give the floor either to the representative of the HVO or of ABiH to know exactly what their final stand would be. And you were there, so you probably heard all this. And we're talking about any topic. You know, X topic, and any meeting. As far as you recollect, was there a representative of HVO that would end the meeting stating the final position of HVO, and the same on the ABiH side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, exactly the way you put it, that would be the structure of these meetings. There were discussions, there were talks, and then some conclusions were reached in a working version, so to speak, and then after both sides accommodated their views, then the representatives of both sides would sign the ultimate agreement. Then I said it was the BH army and the HVO, and I said who the representatives were for the HVO, Tihomir Maric and Slavko Puljic in that period, and on behalf of the BH army, Arif Pasalic and Suad Cupina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, turning now to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, turning now to page 6 of the English version of your 2000 statement and page 8 of the B/C/S version, you mention the conflict between the HVO and ABiH in the Mostar municipality on the 17th of April, 1993. I'd like you, if you will, to take a look at Exhibit 2043.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I don't have that exhibit in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I have it. I have it. 2043.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: We can see that this is a letter of protest signed by Mr. Pasalic to the European Union and UNPROFOR stating the need to address the protest due to the reference of a high-ranking officer of the Croatian army, Slobodan Praljak, in the HVO Main Staff since April 1993, and that he conducts and commands the HVO units, which is against the international regulations. What do you know about this, Mr. Buljko?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document. In that period, that is to say after the 17th of April, there were certain negotiations, and what I know is the following: In the Regional Board of the SDA in Mostar where Mr. Zijad Demirovic was, in the group of people that included Arif Pasalic and Midhad Hujdur, nicknamed Hujka, I think that there were one or two people who came to this Regional Board and that's where I saw Mr. Praljak sitting at the table, whereas Mr. Demirovic was standing. I didn't go into any kind of conversation with Mr. Praljak. I know that he exchanged a few words with Hujka and with Mr. Pasalic. Now, whether that was the reason for this protest addressed to the international forces by Mr. Pasalic, that I don't know. I did see Mr. Praljak sitting there, though, at the regional SDA board in Mostar. This was the period that this protest refers to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And from that experience that you have just recited, do you know in what capacity Mr. Praljak was sitting at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Well, I would not say that it was a formal meeting. As I've already said, I came with this group of people that I have already referred to, and this was very brief. Mr. Pasalic, Hujka, and I were on our feet, so it wasn't that any kind of formal talks were held.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Once again, my question is do you know what capacity Mr. Praljak was there in at this meeting, or informal gathering, if you wish to put it that way?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know. Perhaps it just happened by accident.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: On the same page of your witness statement from 2000, page 6 of the English and 8 of the B/C/S, you describe a meeting that was organised by a Swedish UNPROFOR general between the HVO and ABiH in order it achieve a cease-fire. Do you recall the name of that Swedish UNPROFOR general?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Bo Pellnas.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what was the date of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Around the 20th of April, something like that. Perhaps a bit earlier. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Is this -- the meeting that was organised, were you involved in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes. I took part in these negotiations. I think it had to do with withdrawal from the Mostar Hotel. That is to say, of units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think there were a few more meetings, but Mirza Lakisic, my colleague, attended these other meetings. So as for this specific one, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And who attended at that meeting on behalf of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pasalic. I mean, he was in charge as far as the army of the BH is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And who attended on behalf of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Well, I remember Mr. Tihomir Maric, but I think as far as the military structures are concerned, well, what I can remember now is -- well, that. I think it was Lazic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, turning to page 6 of the English and page 9 of B/C/S statement regarding the HVO offensive that you describe on the 17th of April, 1993, could you now turn to Exhibit 2227. You see this is a letter from the 4th Corps to the president of the republic of BiH mentioning the tense situation in Mostar, people being abused in the wider area of Stolac and Capljina, Mostar being blocked on all sides by the HV and HVO forces so that Serbs and Muslims couldn't leave, and Mostar basically being one huge detention camp for the Muslim people. What do you know about this letter?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this letter. However, as far as the situation is concerned, I think it was described well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: On what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, if I may. Excuse me. The purpose of proofing a witness is to go through the documents and go through their statement.
