I assume that they proofed this witness. And during the proofing session they must have shown the gentleman these documents. Maybe not. Maybe he doesn't recall it. Maybe he's just nervous and he's just unable to remember. But it would seem to me that now we're going -- we're showing him -- we're showing him documents that he's never seen before, therefore, how can he comment on them? I just fail to see. If we go back a couple of questions earlier, she asked him some questions on who was there. In the statement it's very clear. She says Pasalic, and then as far as -- and then Maric for the HVO. And then the gentleman also then says he thinks it was Lazic. I let it go, but if I were doing the direct, I mean, I wouldn't want to be impeaching my own witness, but it seems to me either they haven't met and they haven't proofed or the gentleman is just making things up. And I would suggest at this point that no documents are shown to the witness unless he knows of them, because she can ask him what was the situation in Mostar at that period of time, and then we have his impression. But if they're trying to get this document in, and I would dare say use the word that was used earlier by -- you know, sneak it in, I don't think this is the vehicle, the appropriate manner in doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just observe Your Honour that it was 18 seconds between this witness being asked what he knew about this document and him saying, having acknowledged that he'd never seen it before, that it described the situation well. It's a document that goes on to a second page. This -- supporting Mr. Karnavas's observation, this cannot be the right way to adduce evidence on these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett, this document, this 2227, during the proofing session did you go through this document with the witness? Did you work on the contents? Did the witness say, "Yes, this letter corresponds to the situation at the time"? Or is it the first time that he's actually seen the document? Mr. Karnavas seems to be hinting at that. So has he seen this document previously? Could you please shed some light on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, and it is no surprise that Mr. Karnavas is hinting at this to me. Yes, I went through this document with the witness in the proofing session. Yes, we worked on the contents. Yes, the witness did say that this letter corresponds to the situation at the time. And no, this is not the first time that he is actually seeing the document. And I believe that answers all the questions that Your Honour put in the above paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, either maybe there is -- I misheard it or maybe Ms. Gillett misheard it, but I believe I heard the gentleman say that this is the first time that he's seen this document. And if indeed this is the first time, then what she just said, that it isn't the first time is contrary to what he said. Now, either -- maybe there was a mistranslation, maybe I'm just too tired and I didn't hear it right, but I thought I heard that this was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: He certainly did say that, Your Honour, and I think it is simply a question of a misunderstanding on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Wait a second, hold on. Now she's testifying. How did she know that this was a misunderstanding on the part of the witness? Is she clairvoyant? Let's ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: It's fairly obvious to me what's going on, knowing the situation as I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett, nothing is really that obvious here and you're here to establish facts and the reality of what is being said. Witness, please, have you seen this document? Did you see it yesterday or this morning with Ms. Gillett? Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw this document here in The Hague. When I said I was seeing it for the first time, what I meant was that I hadn't seen it when it was compiled, that is to say on the 8th of May, 1993, that I hadn't seen the document then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If this was shown to him for the very first time when he came to The Hague by Ms. Gillett, then I don't think it's appropriate to elicit testimony from the gentleman, because obviously he didn't know anything about the document before. And we thank him for being honest enough to tell us that this is the very first time, and perhaps he can tell us which other documents he's seeing for the very first time which the Prosecution wishes to adduce at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just add this: The -- I -- when -- when counsel is examining and the witness says something like this, that it's the first time, which obviously, as understood, is going to lead to enormous misunderstanding because it's not so, I do suggest with respect that counsel ought then in the course of examination to make sure, as skilfully and as quickly as possible, that such a misunderstanding is cleared up so that everybody knows. So I do suggest. I apologise to Ms. Gillett and I don't wish to tell her how to do the job, though I once was her head of chambers in London that a question like that would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, many times in my -- I don't know in the last few minutes that this is necessarily true although I think it is, but many times because of the interventions of the counsel, Prosecution counsel is not allowed to get to that step. There is an immediate objection before counsel can go to the next question or ask a clarifying question. Further, it shouldn't be a surprise to anyone in this courtroom at this point, including the Judges, that sometimes the witnesses become confused in the courtroom, sometimes there are translation issues. I've even known some of the Judges to be mistranslated and for us to hear one thing and the witness to have said something else. Now, come on. Let's have a little realism here. Now, my counsel, my colleague should have the chance to clarify the question, and the witness should be given a chance too. That is very stressful situation for everyone, including many of these witnesses, and that also shouldn't come as a surprise to anyone in the courtroom. Further, further, before Judge Trechsel intervenes, further, it doesn't follow at all, it doesn't follow at all, that just because a witness is shown an exhibit for the first time during proofing that the witness can't comment on it. The witness may have been very much involved in the events reflected in the content of the document. The fact that he didn't see the document before, has nothing to do with the propriety of putting that document to the witness. The witness may see a document for the first time and say, Yes, in fact, I was at that very meeting and that's exactly what happened. So the fact that it's shown to the witness for the first time has no bearing whatsoever on the propriety of putting that exhibit to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm troubled by another situation, and that is that if this is the first time that the witness has seen the document in The Hague and if he's commenting on the document to my learned friend of the Prosecution, I'm surprised that we didn't get the document, because it's an addition to the statement. So in -- he couldn't have referred to it if he's seeing it for the first time now, whereas he's commenting on how the document came into being. And I think we should have been informed about that because obviously my learned friend Ms. Gillett is aware of that and informed about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett, while several people were on their feet I was looking a document which I have in front of me. As I read fast, it doesn't take me long to understand. In this letter, Mr. Pasalic is writing to the president of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to Mr. Izetbegovic, undoubtedly, to mention a number of facts. On the face of it, there seem to be some 20 facts mentioned in this letter. So, was he aware of the 20 facts? Was he aware of some of the facts? Ms. Gillett, before mentioning the letter, you could have asked him detailed questions about one or other events. For instance, there were artillery shots in Donja Mahala, in the southern part of Mostar, and so on and so forth. Does he know this? Does he not know this? There is a curfew at 8.00 on the 7th of May. Members of the 4th Corps were captured and released on the same day. A number of facts, a number of facts are mentioned in this letter. Does he know all of the facts or does he know some of the facts? Which of the facts are contained in his written statement, because this document should establish a connection with the written statement. My colleague would also like to say something as a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I think we are accumulating issues here without -- without them being addressed. I think that the point made by Mr. Stewart is quite a reasonable point. I think it would be helpful if the Prosecutor would draw the attention on the -- of the Court to the realities when a witness says that he saw the document for the first time. And this is the third document that he has said this, and before you have not said that. So Mr. Scott's objection that you did not get the time to do it is not -- is not really founded. I think it's a small matter. I quite agree with Mr. Scott that we have had many, many times witnesses testifying on documents they had not seen before proofing, before being in contact with the OTP, and we have rules on this, and normally, I think that should not be a special issue. I think you could proceed now, Ms. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, on page 9 of the B/C/S version of your statement and page 6 of the English version, you speak about events on the 9th of May, 1993, saying that you were woken up by HVO soldiers wearing black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett, I'm a little bit lost. The document which has been -- just been discussed, and we've wasted 10 minutes on this, is what occurred on the 8th -- on the 8th of May and the days prior to that. You're now moving on to the 9th of May. Are you moving on to another topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, all right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Page 9 of the B/C/S, as I said, page 6 of the English, 9th of May. Mr. Buljko, you say that you were woken up by HVO soldiers wearing black uniforms. What --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What colour was the HVO uniform at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: They were uniforms, camouflage military uniforms as we referred to them, but the individual who threw me out of my flat and woke me up at 5.00 a.m. was wearing a black uniform, which might have looked like a HOS, H-O-S, uniform. Well, it was some officer in charge of throwing people out, probably because he had been trained to do so. Now, who he actually belonged to, whether Tuta, Stela or the HVO, or whatever, I don't know, but he belonged to one of those units who were in charge of throwing people out be the 9th of May at 5.00 a.m. Thousands of Bosnian Muslims were evicted and I was thrown out in my pyjamas with nothing on my feet. We were rounded up in front of the building. They referred to us in derogatory terms. They called us balijas, and I don't think they even knew what balija meant. Perhaps they'd heard from each other. People called each other balijas. But anyway, we were rounded up in front of our buildings, all of our groups in front of the entrance to each building, and we had to obey their orders. We had to crouch, to kneel down, and wait and see what would happen to us. When I crouched down, I saw soldiers around my building without any insignia whatsoever on their uniforms. So I didn't know whether they were soldiers of the Croatian army or the HVO or whatever. And they had RPGs and were standing round my building. And I wondered why they had these RPGs and why they were cocking them at unarmed civilians. And later on, I saw that two or three entrances away from my entrance, they'd already started killing the civilians. The previous night, on the 8th of May, and I was living at Balinovac at the time or Vucja Jazbina as it was called, the Fox's Lair, and I was a witness to all these events. So that night on the 8th of May, thousands of vehicles from Siroki Brijeg or Listica, as it used to be called, arrived in Mostar and looking at all this from my window, I wondered where all those cars were going. And then there was a restaurant near my building and I saw that soldiers were gathering together by that restaurant, that they were drinking and I knew that something was going to happen. And knowing of the tensions that prevailed during those days, it was quite clear to me that what was to happen was going to happen, and after they rounded us up, this group of people who was a -- the group that was the first to be evicted from their flats --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you speak a little bit slower, less fast, because the interpreters are -- they are coping still, but one feels that they are hard pressed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, getting to that point, you mention then in your statement, talking about your forcible eviction on the 9th of May, page 6 still of the English and 9 of the B/C/S, you mention other Muslims being forced to go in the opposite direction to the one that you went in, being led to the stadium, the Stadion. What was this Stadion?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: It's the city stadium. So when we went to Semovac with this first group of people, we were told to go there. I saw a lot of people who had been evicted from the high-rise building, and there are some 60 residences in each of the high-rise buildings times the number of family members would make it 200 inhabitants from just one high-rise, and there were seven or eight of them. It was Franjevacka Ulica and had a different name previously, so the residents from the Matija Gubac Street were moving towards the city Stadion. And they told us, the friends that I saw along the way, moving towards the direction of the city Stadion, said they had been ordered to rally at the Stadion. However, I passed by that same street, and luckily it's a flat street, so I reached Semovac and rushed across to that part at Semovac, well, there were business buildings and my company was located there, the one that threw me out. Anyway, when I crossed this area I had to stop twice because I heard some shots coming from some PAM weapons firing above, somewhere at Hum or Panjevina. That's the area that I passed by. So I had to run across and my heart was pounding. I was never as afraid as I was at that moment. I thought that the PAMs were shooting at me and a lot of elderly people who could barely walk crossed over to Semovac that day, but the shelling started very soon, as well, of East Mostar --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, sorry to interrupt you. If I could ask you, do you know what happened to the people that were taken to the Stadion?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: According to what the people told me and what my mother and sister told me, my mother was 73 years old at the time, and she was also taken off to the Stadion from another part of town, from the avenue. She went to the city Stadion, and she told me what was happening there and what happened at Heliodrom when she was incarcerated there. So I heard this from my mother and from my sister. I have the exact information. I know how many people were held at the city stadium and how many were taken to Heliodrom. So that's as regards my family. Now, as to other witnesses, I had thousands of statements from people who were forcibly evicted and displaced within Mostar and who told me how they were taken out of their flats and where they found themselves afterwards. They found themselves in the concentration camps as we called them, the HVO concentration camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, how did you come to have thousands of statements from people who were forcibly evicted and displaced in Mostar? How did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Our civilian police force collected the statements, collected statements from most of the displaced persons and the refugees who were there during that period of time, who arrived in June and July 1992. And what happened was that all these people had lost their property. So this lost property was reported as you do everywhere, in the West and in the East. You report lost property.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How did you come to be in possession of the statements that civilian police force had collected?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: In my capacity as coordinator for humanitarian activities, and also in my capacity in the Department for Displaced Persons and Refugees in Herzegovina, without Konjic and Jablanica, I'm referring to displaced persons from the Mostar area, as well as Capljina, Stolac, Ljubuski, and so on, who were in East Mostar at the time, I had personal contacts with those people. I came into contact with them personally. And I talked to them, and they told me their stories. They told me what had happened to them from the 9th of May onwards. And secondly, the statements that I mentioned, well, our police force summarised them because I cooperated with the civilian police in order to resolve the situation and the problems that displaced persons and refugees had. I mean, the persons who were in Mostar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, we'll come back a little bit later on to your role as the coordinator for displaced persons and refugees. Turning to page 7 of the English statement and 10 of the B/C/S statement. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. A point of clarification. I'm interrupting now because otherwise we might forget about it. I was quite struck by the fact you mentioned that on the 8th of May, there were thousands of cars seemingly that had reached Mostar, and on the 8th of May you seemed to have seen a lot of soldiers around in bars, so you thought that something was afoot. That's the first time, because we have been hearing witnesses here for the past year on the question of Mostar, it's the first time that I hear a great number of cars reached Mostar. Are you sure that on the 8th of May you saw a great many cars entering Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I said is the truth. I lived in Balinovac in a building which overlooks the road leading from the cemetery, the olive grove cemetery to Siroki Brijeg, and from my window that night, late at night on the 8th of May, I saw thousands of car lights, cars coming into Mostar. And as for the soldiers, they had already taken their -- taken control of the restaurant belonging to Jusa Dizdarevic. They had evicted his family before that and the man hasn't visited his restaurant to that day. So they'd already taken over that restaurant late on the 8th of May. .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these cars, you saw thousands of lights from these cars. Where were these cars coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the direction of Siroki Brijeg. From Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 8th of May and this is in your statement. If I don't put you the question I am not doing my job properly, and as I have every intention of doing my job very well, I'm going to put the question to you. On page 6, you say -- you mention the SpaBat, and you say that on the 8th of May, according to what you think, you say, "I believe they had left their positions in Mostar to move 20 kilometres away," and you say that you didn't know why they had repositioned their camps. If you have mentioned this, I assume you witnessed this with your own eyes. Why, according to you, did the SpaBat leave Mostar on the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. I saw them withdraw, because I didn't see them in Mostar that day, so they must have withdrawn. That's why I say I believe, because I didn't know what was going to happen the following day. Now, when the conflict began on the 9th of May, they were not in Mostar. Perhaps they were on the surrounding hills. I don't know that. That's just an assumption on my part. But later on from the statements that the representatives of the international community made, I learnt from what they said, I learnt that they had withdrawn to their camp in Medjugorje which is some 20 kilometres away from Mostar. And then later on they appeared in the Mostar area, some five or six or four or five days later. I'm not quite sure. So the Spanish Battalion left the civilians of Mostar. The Spanish Battalion did not accomplish its assignment. And it was UNPROFOR, the protection forces, that's what it was supposed to be. It was cowardly of them to leave Mostar at that point in time, and they appeared later on after the international community had exerted pressure on them to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my last question now on the 8th and 9th of May. On the 8th of May you were still the official interpreter of Mr. Pasalic at the international meetings he attended; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see Mr. Pasalic on the 8th. He wasn't there then. I don't think he was in Mostar then. At least I didn't see him on the eve of the 9th of May, as far as I remember. And I don't think he was in Mostar. Later on I heard that he was held somewhere, but I don't know. I didn't discuss it with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You belonged to the 41st Brigade, didn't you? Where was the camp of the 41st Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasalic was the commander of the 4th Corps of the BH army. I was a member of the 41st famed Motorised Brigade which had a logistical unit in the Vranica building which is where the command of the 4th Corps was located. So we were in the cellar and they were, I think, on the ground floor, or a mezzanine floor of the Vranica building. So in another part. Whereas the BH army units were in South Camp. They were in the Mostar Hotel prior to that and in some other buildings, but that was mostly where the units of the 41st famed Motorised Brigade were located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 8th of May did you go into the Vranica building to see your colleagues and your friends? On the 8th of May did you enter the building, the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 8th of May, I was with a colleague of mine who was cleaning up his house. He was restoring his house. So I didn't appear on the 8th of May in the Vranica building, but I was there on the 7th of May, and I know that people were doing shift work and duty work, that is to say, members of the BH army at that time. They were on duty in the Vranica building. But specifically on the 8th of May, I did not appear on those premises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can imagine the following military situation: The ABiH, the 41st Motorised Brigade receives an order to attack the HVO on the 9th or the 8th of May. If there had been such an order, would you yourself been prepared to take up an assignment? And you would have been mobilised, as you were, in the Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me say something first of all, something about the attack of the brigade or the corps of the BH army. Well, there can be no mention of an attack, because the army and corps in Mostar had very little materiel and equipment. So they couldn't stand up to the much mightier force that came into Mostar, the Croatian army and the Croatian Defence Council. So this assumption --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let him answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is untenable. Now, as far as whether I would have been there -- whether I was there, well, I would have been in the Vranica building had I been on assignment there, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to make one observation. First, the gentleman obviously is speaking to his audience in Mostar, and maybe too, because he's a consultant, maybe he's promoting himself. I would appreciate if he would simply answer your questions. Your questions are very precise, and I think that the gentleman is playing games. You understand me, sir. So please just answer the questions and we'll get along fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. My question was the following: If there had been an attack, you would have been present. So answer in two stages -- you answered in two stages. You said ABiH didn't have time to react. But if there had been an order, you would have been present and not, you know, doing something else somewhere else. So what about General Pasalic? Where was he on May 8?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was not in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you had no idea where he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there was -- there was a response to the question that was not recorded, or it was not in the transcript. What was the first answer you gave to the President when he asked you whether you would have been present at the -- at the HQ if there had been a plan to attack? Did you say yes or no or something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The planned attack by the BH army? Well, as far as I understood it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The hypothetical. If assuming that there was such a plan, would you have been at the office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, turning to page 7 of the English version of your statement and page 10 of the B/C/S. You mention a meeting between the HVO, the main representative of whom being Mr. Petkovic, and the ABiH, the main representative being Mr. Halilovic, and attend by UNPROFOR Lieutenant-General Morillon and Ambassador Thebault with the purpose of agreeing on the cessation of hostilities in BiH. Did you attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I was not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, that being your answer, we see in your statement that you then go on to give a number of details about the agreement, so my question to you is: How did you come to know of these details that you describe in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: On the 25th of May, we had negotiations on the realisation of the agreement on cessation of hostilities. In the meantime, in this delegation consisting of Lieutenant-General Philippe Morillon, representative of UNPROFOR, and Sefer Halilovic, commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who had come to Mostar to inform the representatives of the military authorities, that is to say the 4th Corps and the 41st glorious Brigade on the agreement reached, I got hold of this document that was provided in order to know what was discussed and what was dealt with at the meeting of the HVO and the ABiH on the 12th of May. It was very important, because it gave some hope, primarily in terms of releasing civilians who were detained in prisons and with regard to further activities. So I got a hold of this document which was no secret to the mentioned gentlemen, has to say Brigadier Budakovic and Mr. Midhad Hujdur, Hujka, who attended the meeting then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you take a look at Exhibit 2352. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: This is the document of the 12th of May, the agreement on a cessation of hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina concluded between General Milivoj Petkovic and General Sefer Halilovic in the presence of Lieutenant-General Philippe Morillon, and the representative of ECMM, that is, Jean-Pierre Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, on the same page of your statement that I mentioned previously, page 7 of the English and page 10 of the B/C/S, and in relation to this exhibit that I've just shown you, 2352, you mention in your statement -- you provide further information as to compliance or lack thereof with this agreement. Where did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Specifically these are articles of the agreement on the cessation of hostilities that were in force at that point in time. Freedom of movement. I have already said -- yes, well, a reference is made to those two roads, but as for any kind of realisation, that did not actually take place. It was only the southern route that was used for bringing humanitarian aid. The northern one never was used. As for Article 2 --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, where did you get that information from? How did you know that that did not take place? You just mention in relation to Article 1, that it did not take place. How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Well, because we were not receiving humanitarian aid from the beginning of the conflict, the 9th of May, all the way up to the 25th of August. I knew that at that point in time. There was no aid coming in. That is what I knew. So that was number one. Number two, I was glad that the battalion finally returned to Mostar, and I said that here as well. I said that that was favourable regarding this agreement on the cessation of hostilities. And I said that I saw the Spanish Battalion sometime around the 13th or 14th of May. I already said that the armed forces regrouped. In some places they withdrew, but that was also temporary. As for the release of prisoners, I said that there were 20 Bosnian Croats who were detained by the ABiH, but we knew that there were tens of thousands of Bosnian Muslims at the Heliodrom. And I knew that not all persons from the Heliodrom were released in that period of time. Or let me be more specific. First the elderly and infirm were released, like my mother. She was released -- among the first people who were released. Also the ill people were released. Then slowly others were being released as well. However, the Heliodrom still remained -- or, rather, not all prisoners were released at the time as was agreed in this agreement. As for displaced persons --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise for interrupting, but I think that this will be a useful intervention for all of us. The witness told us that as for this agreement, he learned of it on the 25th of May, 1993, when the meeting was held, and that at that point in time the gentlemen provided information on this agreement that was reached on the 12th of May. So now I would kindly ask when the witness is telling us about the realisation or the lack thereof of some articles of the agreement from the 12th of May, could he tell us from what point of view or, rather, from what date he is speaking about the realisation or non-realisation of this agreement, because if he's talking about the 25th of May, that is going to be one thing, and it's going to be quite different if he's talking about the 15th of May. So if you could kindly clarify that for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you did not hear me right. I said that this happened when Lieutenant-General Morillon and Mr. Sefer Halilovic came to the command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina where I attended part of the talks, where the agreement was brought but on the 25th of May, of course the document was provided yet again because what is referred to is realisation of the agreement, this agreement that we are talking about. As for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps you have not quite understood the question of the lawyer, Ms. Alaburic. The question is you are now telling us that the agreement of the 12th May was not complied with. Do you say so on the basis of your recollection of the situation, let us say, on the 15th of May, or do you tell us this in your recollection of the 25th of May or some other date? It's really a question of a date. I hope I correctly repeated your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour, Judge Trechsel. I would just like to point out, Witness, that what you said here was, if I understood you correctly, that you did not attend the meeting on the 12th of May where the agreement was adopted, the one that we're discussing now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. I was not present on the 12th, but I was present when Mr. Morillon was there, Mr. Sefer Halilovic, and on the 25th of May. As for the comments I made, they pertain in part from the period from the 25th of May, and in part, to what I said referred to the return of displaced persons and that pertained to my statement of the year 2000. They had not even returned then, and not everybody had returned on the -- in the year 2000, either. I got my property back in 2000, mid-2000. I made my statement in 2000. So part of it has to do with the period up to the 25th of May, and there's yet another part that pertains to what had not been implemented even 10 years after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Ms. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, in relation to what you say about implementation of this agreement, do you know who was responsible for implementing the agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Well, the signatories are responsible for implementing the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise, but in view of this question, I think it would be fair to the witness and to the Trial Chamber to ask the witness whether he knows on the basis of what this agreement was reached in the first place, because two days earlier on, there were statements made by Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic, the top people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 10th of May, 1993. So that would be a full answer to the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps some of these questions could be saved for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think you're quite right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, moving on, you mentioned further in your statement an agreement on the deployment of the UN civil police monitors to the Mostar area on the 19th of May, 1993, and you mention that at page 8 of the English version of the statement and page 11 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How did you come by this agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Through UN CIVPOL, through their representative, and the representatives of our police, because I attended -- or, rather, interpreted meetings between the UN CIVPOL and the civilian police at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recall when those meetings were?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Sometime after the 20th of May -- or, rather, the 19th of May, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you recall who attended those meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: The representatives of our civilian police, I think it was Mr. Ramo Maslesa, Mr. Adnan Jusufbegovic and Mr. Zuljevic who were members of the civilian police anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you take a look at Exhibit 2460, please. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: This has to do with the mandate of the civilian police of the UN for the Mostar area. That is to say, their deployment in the area of Mostar from the 19th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And once again you relay information in your statement on the implementation of this agreement at page 8 of the English and 11 and 12 of the B/C/S. Now, regarding this information that you relay on implementation, you have numbered points in your statement 1 to 6. How did you find out about these points that you've numbered 1 to 6 regarding implementation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I'll start from the end. Article 6, they did not manage to assist the efforts of humanitarian aid agencies to enter Mostar due to the blockade of the HVO. That's true. We insisted. We asked, we beseeched the international community, all the representatives and, you see here, even the civilian police, to help the people who had come without clothing, without footwear, without money to the then Eastern Mostar. I made a statement and said that after three or four months, on the 25th of August -- well, we'll get to that subject too. The first convoy of humanitarian aid arrived for 55.000 inhabitants of East Mostar. That is number 6. As for the other points, according to the talks held with the representatives of the civilian police of the UN and our civilian police, they said that up to a certain degree they could supervise the activities of the local police. The joint patrols were not possible because it was dangerous for the representatives of the UN civilian police. That's true. There was terrible fighting going on then. There was shelling. Mostar was being shelled. So it was impossible to patrol, that's true. And it is also true that from time to time there were independent patrols when this was made possible by the situation in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, do you remember names of any of the representatives that you held talks with from the UN civilian police or indeed the -- your own civilian police?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I've already mentioned our civilian police representatives, and I remember Mr. Albert Benabou who was a representative of the UN civilian police in our area. And there were other people there, too, but I think that Mr. Benabou was the key person in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Once again from the meetings and discussions whereby you learnt of this agreement, are you able to say, do you know who was responsible for the implementation of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Are you referring to the agreement of the 19th of May concerning the civilian police? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Buljko, that's right.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: As for the implementation as regards the civilian police, I know it was Ramo Maslesa. And in the HVO -- now, was it Mr. Valentin Coric? If this has to do with the civilian police, it has to do with people who were in charge on behalf of the civilian police to implement this agreement together with the UN CIVPOL police.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, turning to the agreement on the 25th of May, 1993, that you mention at page 8 of the English version of the statement and page 12 of the B/C/S version. Were you present for the negotiations with respect to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you turn to Exhibit 02 -- sorry, 2512. 2512.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes. Realisation of the agreement on cessation of hostilities between General Petkovic and General Sefer Halilovic, the 12th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, once again in your statement at the same page as previously mentioned, 8 of the English and 12 of the B/C/S, you comment on the outcome of this agreement. How did you come to know of the outcome of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: 25th of May, 1993. What was requested was the release of all civilians who were in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise, but I don't know if the witness is now reading or if he's talking about an agreement that he saw earlier on, because two minutes ago he said that he is looking a document that was signed by Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Halilovic. However, we have the document of the 25th of May in front of us, and now we have an agreement in front of us that was signed by completely different people as negotiators. I really don't know what he's talking about now, and I don't know whether the witness is aware of what document he's looking at. I think Ms. Gillett has to look at this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that this had to do with the realisation of the agreement signed on the 12th of May, whereas this is the 25th of May, 1993. And that is precisely what I wish to comment upon or to explain the comments that I gave in my statement for the Honourable Trial Chamber. Now, should I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's your Witness, Ms. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. Sadly, not usually me who decides, but I'd be grateful to the witness if he would proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, you were about to explain in relation to this Exhibit 2512.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have some direction? I think the witness is unclear as to what it is he's being asked to say about this agreement, and frankly, so am I. I think one of the problems we've had throughout this case is that we seem to always be -- have the second eleven playing here. I mean, we have an interpreter commenting on the contents and implementation of a very fundamental document. It's hard to understand, but at least perhaps Ms. Gillett could make it clear to the witness what we expect to get from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Gillett, ask him first whether he was present when the agreement was signed, whether he saw the documents being signed, what the parties said, whether there was difficulties in reaching an agreement and so forth. I think this document has already been tendered. We already have seen all these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The document has been admitted, not tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, in relation to this Exhibit 2512, were you present as part of the negotiating team in relation to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean -- I think -- now the question is whether he was there as part of the negotiating team. He was there to translate. He was there to exchange -- you know, as a conduit, you know, from one language to the next, not to negotiate, and that's what the problem is that was raised and has been raised. He's not in a position. I know the gentleman would like to be able to comment but he was just there translating. And now asking him about who was supposed to be implementing and what were the results, this can be achieved by getting a narration from the gentleman. If he was there in situ, what did he see? What did he observe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I will have the feeling that we are beating about the bush a little bit without achieving anything. On the 25th of May there is a meeting which is being held together with Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Halilovic, and there are two high-ranking members of the international community, General Morillon and the Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault. So on the ABiH side there is Mr. Pusic and Mr. Pasalic and also other members whose names are mentioned. So you were an interpreter at the time the document was signed. You said you were there, but before they signed was there a speech? Do you remember what positions they held? Were there any difficulties that were raised, given that you were a witness? You could hear what was going on. Did the things run smoothly? Was it easy to sign the document or were there any hiccups even though you yourself were not party to the negotiation of this document? Ms. Alaburic, [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but the question contains something that does not fully reflect what it was that was going on. On the 25th of May, 1993, a meeting was not held that was attended by Generals Petkovic and Halilovic. Rather, this meeting on the 25th of May was held between Mr. Puljic and Mr. Pasalic, and the meeting was held in order to see how the agreement would be implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite right. You are quite right. The meeting of the 25th of May was the implementation of the 12th of May. In other words, the people whose name are mentioned in the document, which is about to be signed on the HVO side by Pusic [as interpreted] and Maric and the ABiH side signed by Pasalic and Cupina. So at this meeting on the 25th of May do you remember whether the participants raised any difficulties? Were there any problems and so on and so forth, or did everybody sign without question anything -- questioning anything whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. I don't wish to interrupt either you or the witness, but I think there's just a mistake in the transcript because the signatory was not Mr. Pusic but Mr. Puljic, which we can see from the document, LJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you answer the question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this negotiating team signed something that was very significant at that point in time, and what we were concerned about most was that all the civilians should be allowed to go home. Now, furthermore, I know that they were allowed to go home because I know that people did in fact go home, both on the west bank and the east bank at that short period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you're not answering the question. I'm not interested to know whether this document is an important document or not. I would like to know how this meeting of the 25th of May unfolded. Perhaps one of the negotiators said it was important. That is my question. I don't want your opinion on the matter. I would like to know what you heard from what the negotiators.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as this document is concerned, the talks were difficult. However, they did bear fruit. And I don't think there were any major outstanding problems for which this document could not be signed. And the situation proved that, after the signing of this agreement reached between the two negotiating parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have a tendency to give us your point of view when we're talking about events that involve other people. I didn't ask you what you thought about it. I asked you whether there were any difficulties during that meeting, whether the document was signed without any problems. This is my question. So had the document been drafted prior to the meeting? Had it already been printed out and the negotiators only had to sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the negotiations were lengthy, and ultimately this agreement was arrived at, and that the two parties signed it. So what preceded was the procedure of negotiation in order to reach agreement along with assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that it took a long time, but what time did the meeting start? At what time did it end? At what time did people sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't remember the exact time. A lot of time has elapsed and the meetings were usually in the morning at 10.00 or 11.00, and they would conclude depending on the circumstances, depending on the topics under discussion, whether they were difficult discussions, difficult issues to resolve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But as you remember, there was Peter Espensen and Nigel Milverton, two representatives of the international community. Did they take part, did they intervene, did they state their positions, or were they people who just signed? And were these two people chairing the meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The international community, the witnesses, mostly chaired. Now, the HVO and the BH army negotiated at those meetings. They discussed the issues, and I think that this is a joint document compiled on the basis of negotiations between both sides along with the assistance or testimony from Mr. Milverton and the other man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you say, I believe, that this was the outcome of the negotiations. So you did not attend the negotiations. You didn't witness the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was witness to the negotiations in my capacity of interpreting for the representatives of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question before we have a break. You tell us that you were an interpreter. During the negotiation process, did you translate for both sides, the positions put forward by Mr. Pasalic and Mr. Pusic, or did you translate the positions of the representatives of the international community? Did you translate all of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly I translated what was said by the BH army representatives. On rare occasions, I interpreted for everyone, including the HVO and what the witnesses testifying said about the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question that the Prosecution should have put to you right from the outset, what about the HVO? Did they have their own interpreter, because the HVO might not have trusted you. Did they come along with their own interpreter? If you were the ABiH interpreter, did the HVO also have their own interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that there were some young ladies that appeared at the meetings. I don't know if they were official interpreters or whether they accompanied somebody attending, but anyway, there were people there translating for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's a quarter to. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, just to finish with this exhibit that we were looking at prior to the break, Exhibit 2512, once again at the -- at the meeting that you attended with respect to these negotiations, what, if anything, was discussed as regards implementation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes, with respect to the cessation of hostilities and the agreement was signed between the BH army, General Sefer Halilovic signed; for the HVO General Milivoj Petkovic. It was the 12th of May, 2005. No, what I meant to say was 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: In relation to the exhibit that we see in front of us, 2512, what was discussed as far as this is concerned, this document?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: We discussed the release of civilians from the camp, and that anybody who wished to cross from the left to the right bank need to sign, and that buses would be provided. I was involved after this meeting in the procedure. We had a list of civilians who wished to cross over from the west bank, the Djacki Dom, and we had a list of civilians in a facility near the Razvitak department store. And I helped out, and I went with the buses on those two days. I think that's how long it lasted. That is to say, after the 25th of May. So it was towards the end of May. I went to both sides with the buses. So I went to the Djacki Dom and helped out there, helped the civilians there, and were given lists of names by the HVO representatives. And I was also at the Razvitak department store helping them, civilians, and was given lists of their names, and then I went with them across to the right bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Moving on to page 9 of the English version of your statement and 13 of the B/C/S version. You mention here another agreement from the 8th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: That was the further implementation of the agreement on a cessation to the hostilities, and that was signed between Generals Milivoj Petkovic and Sefer Halilovic on the 12th of May. And the meeting was attended by Mr. Pasalic and Mr. Puljic, Slavko Puljic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you attend this particular meeting in relation to the 8th of June, 1993, agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you take a look at Exhibit 2680. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: This is another agreement in a series, which was a little more voluminous than the previous one, a little more detailed, and it looked into the problems of expelled persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just to hold you there for a moment in the interests of clarity. When you say this is another agreement in a series, are you saying -- what do you mean by that? Are you saying it is different to the agreement that you reference on page 9 of your statement, or is it one and the same as the agreement mentioned on page 9 of your statement as being the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: This is the continuation of the negotiations and the agreement reached on the 8th of June, 1993, which is much broader in scope. A lot of the same issues, like the previous one on the 25th of May, but much broader in scope and going in-depth, especially with respect to the problems facing the civilian population. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you say that you were at this meeting. In your statement you also comment on the outcome of the agreement that was reached at that meeting. How do you know what the outcome of the agreement was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: As this had to do with displaced civilians mostly, refugees, and questions of humanitarian aid, already at that time I had been given certain assignments, that is to say, to coordinate humanitarian activities faced with that situation, and I was well-informed, especially with respect to the humanitarian situation and the civilian population in East Mostar. I know that some of the points mentioned in this agreement that was reached on the 8th of June, 1993, did not -- were not carried out or implemented, because I know that a commission was never set up to assess the damages. And as far as the prisoners or detainees was concerned, not all the prisons that existed at that time under HVO control were allowed to be visited. Some were; some weren't. I heard that later from witnesses, too, people who had been incarcerated and who told me about this. They said that they never saw anybody come to them from the international community, from the International Red Cross committee or whatever. They might have gone to visit later. So they never came into contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: From your attendance at the meeting in relation to this agreement, do you know who was responsible for implementation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: There are 12 points here --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Objection, Your Honour. Hold on, sir. The question was rather precise. It calls for a yes or no, and then he can answer. So if we could get the answer first and then if he wishes to expand I'm sure Madam Prosecutor would know exactly what questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Witness, answer the question. The question was who was in charge of implementing the agreement, and you're saying there are 12 points. That's your answer. But before giving us that kind of answer, tell us who was in charge of implementing the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, with respect, Your Honour, the question was does he know. It is a prior question, and Your Honour's question may then be the next question depending upon what the witness's answer is to that prior question. That's the one to which Mr. Karnavas was correctly suggesting there could be a simple yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So, Witness, please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question -- to answer Mr. Karnavas's question, yes, I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] No, the question was the Prosecution's question, and answer the Prosecution's question. You're not here to do your work for Mostar. This is not a political forum. This is what I object to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: There's absolutely no basis for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There's no reason to -- he answered, in fact, Ms. Gillett's question because you had insisted that it should be answered, and it was the same answer. So there's no reason to complain. So your answer, Mr. Witness, you have said, yes, you knew who was -- or you know who was responsible for the implementation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is correct. Not only the signatories, Arif Pasalic and Slavko Puljic, but here it was a question of very serious subjects and issues, and it had to do with East Mostar in 1993. So in all the structures, both the BH army and the HVO, there were individuals who were in charge of certain questions, certain fields. We knew who was in charge of displaced persons, for example, and who was in charge of others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... But let's not waste any time. I've noted the following: The -- this agreement of June 8 is number two, but when I look at the B/C/S version, I don't see a signature on the HVO side. So in the end this agreement seemed not to have been signed by HVO, and there's no mention of international witnesses. In the document number one there were international witnesses, but here the box for international witnesses is empty. So did the agreement actually exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The version that I have, you can see that you have some things written in hand. This is Mr. Suad Cupina's handwriting. And he also attended the meeting but did not sign this particular agreement. It was just signed by Mr. Arif Pasalic. So this agreement was reached, with the amendments introduced in writing, handwritten amendments.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the sake of clarity, unless I'm mistaken as to Your Honour's point, the signatures at the bottom of the B/C/S version are neither signatures from the HVO nor from the ABiH. Your Honour may note the date of the 10th of July, 2000, and a signature above that. I'm not sure whether that was the signature to which Your Honour was referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're saying that Mr. Cupina signed, but I have no document bearing his signature. The document that you handed over seems to be a document that you had with you, but it's only the copy of another document that had been signed by Mr. Cupina. The document we have here bears -- does not bear the signature of Mr. Cupina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that I received this version from Mr. Suad Cupina, who attended the negotiations, but he didn't sign. It was Mr. Slavko Puljic and Mr. Arif Pasalic who signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we don't have the authentic one, and he got it from Mr. Cupina, whose character is -- has come into question, I don't see any point in going into this document any longer. I just -- and when was it that he received this document from Mr. Cupina? And it's just -- we seem to be going in circles. Either he was there or he wasn't. If he was there, he would have been able to -- to obtain the document, and he would be able to tell us. But if you look at the document, obviously it doesn't comport with what he's telling us. Then later on he gets it from Cupina. Was Cupina also there? In what capacity? I just think we're getting too -- we're trying to get too much out of this particular witness. The documents can come in through some other witness but not through this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Witness, you're saying that Mr. Cupina gave you this document. When did he give you this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 8th of June, 1993, when the negotiations were completed. And that was the first version without the additions written in hand. And I received a version that was the final version and which the two parties signed with the additions that were introduced in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. But to your knowledge, this document, you say it's the final draft, but to your knowledge was this document, this final draft signed by everyone? And you saw them sign the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the final version with the corrections, and this document was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this document coming in, or I would object to this gentleman talking about this document. Obviously he had plenty of time in 2002 to search for and look for and -- from 2000, to provide this document. Obviously Mr. Cupina is his friend. He could certainly get the document, or from one of the negotiators, but I don't think -- first of all, we don't know whether this was the final version. We have no signatures. There's nothing here other than what he's telling us. And I dare say his word alone is insufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is why I took the floor, to state that we also have -- we have document number two. Document number one is signed but, document number two bears no signature. So if it has been signed, there must be another copy someplace with the signatures. Ms. Gillett --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just add a word, I'm sorry. There seem to have been witnesses, Messrs. Morillon and Thebault, but is there any reason why they're not mentioned where there is a space for witnesses? Why is this blank? Is there any explanation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I would like the witness to answer this question. Do you have an explanation, Witness, as to why on this document the names of the witnesses are not where the space is open for these names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the simple reason that this is the final working version, which then went out to be typed and was then signed, and then the witnesses were added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all I wanted to do was to say that Mr. Morillon and Mr. Thebault were mentioned in the text because they were the co-signatories of an agreement of the 12th of May, 1993, which it does indeed say in the introductory paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please resume, Ms. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, you had mentioned some time ago now that you were aware of who was responsible for the implementation of this agreement, but I don't believe, if I remember correctly, that you were given the opportunity to mention any names, if you're able to recall any names of the -- of persons who you were aware were responsible for implementation of this agreement. So are you able to provide any names of persons that were responsible for the implementation of this agreement? I believe you also had stated that it wasn't just the signatories.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: That's right. It wasn't the signatories. It was people who were put in charge of certain questions to which the agreement refers, signed by the negotiating team, the team for implementation, the agreement that we mentioned quite a few times already. And I want to say that as far as the refugees and displaced persons are concerned, they agreed that each side on their side, that is to say the HVO and the BH army, would, through their own services and offices, implement what was written in the agreement. Now, as far as food was concerned --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just to pause there briefly, Mr. Buljko. You mention it was agreed that each side, the HVO and the BH army, would, through their own services and offices, implement what was written in the agreement. Do you know of the names of any individuals that were in charge for doing this?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: As far as the BH army is concerned, I do know that for a fact. But as far as the HVO is concerned, well, there were services and offices and departments dealing with humanitarian issues. As far as theft was concerned or looting, I said that the commission was never established.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You just mentioned refugees and displaced persons previously. Do you know who was responsible for that particular area from the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I can't remember just now. It's rather complex. It will probably come to me in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, as far as the other areas involved in the agreement were concerned, do you have any names of the individuals who were responsible for the other areas that were involved in the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. I didn't want to intervene before, but this is the situation that we had earlier on when you said, Don't let the witness leave the court and then have the witness shown documents and so on. Mr. Cupina was here. He could have asked him about the document, and now they're trying, through this witness, to clear the situation up. So my objection is if Mr. Cupina is here, he could have explained everything with respect to this agreement to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but the witness is also present at a meeting regarding this agreement. He's also in a position, not the same position, but in a position to be able to provide some information on the agreement, and it is up to the Prosecution what they wish to ask the witness in that respect. Not every witness gives the same information, although the same documents are able to be used with different witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Witness, on page 11 of the English version of your statement and page 16 of the B/C/S version, you mention a request by Alija Alikadic that urge the local communities to collect and submit complete personal data in relation to certain issues that you number at 1 to 4 of that same page -- same pages that I've mentioned. Could you turn to Exhibit 4102. And is this the same document that you reference in your statement and indeed that you hand over to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you detail in your statement at that same page how you came to be in possession of this request when you were appointed the head of the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees for Herzegovina. On what date were you appointed the head of Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees for Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I was appointed on the 23rd of September. However, as I've already said, I was involved with the civilian authorities on the territory of the then East Mostar the end of June. So already by July, we were establishing civilian authorities, and I was involved in humanitarian matters. So in a way this had to do with that field of work even before the 23rd of September, my appointment. And also, we collected information about detainees, prisoners, displaced persons, displaced persons living in territory controlled by the BH army, and persons who were wounded during the war operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, on what date did you get a copy of this request?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I got it on the same day, the 11th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mention in your statement that you became responsible for the follow-up to this request, and you touched on that just now. I don't propose to go into further detail exactly because it's covered in the statement. However, leading on from that, can you turn to Exhibits -- Exhibit 4888. Can you describe what this is, what this document is?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: This is a series of documents that local communes in the then East Mostar had compiled on the basis of the requests that we discussed a few moments ago, namely the 11th of August, 1993. In view of the fact that the situation was extremely difficult, we didn't have any electricity or basic living conditions, some local communes had a typewriter, others did not. Most of the documents were written in hand, and they deal with these four questions -- or, rather, these four requests for collecting information about the persons that the document of the 11th of August refers to. So all the local communes that existed in Mostar then submitted to me information that was supposed to be stored on computer hard disks. On the basis of that, four lists were compiled on the basis of that request. As you can see, quite a bit of this information is rather exhaustive: Date of birth, father's name, where the said person was at that point in time when the document was written. I see here a document dated the 8th of September, 1993. It was compiled by Sadeta Ahmetovic from the Carina local commune. So this is an addendum to the list she had provided previously. So you can see that Mr. Salih Golos, son of Ibre, born in 1938, was in the Heliodrom from the 30th of July, 1993. Then Mr. Tinjak Ahmet, born in '44 from Hodbine was in Dretelj from the 1st of July, 1993, and so on and so forth. So I have handed this over to the Honourable Trial Chamber. There are many original documents that came from local communes, from the people who were in charge of collecting such data. The process was a rather lengthy one and could not have been completed in the requested period, the period requested in the letter, that is, but I think that we did manage to obtain some finalised lists of these categories of the population who were in these four situations at that point in time, August and September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, in relation to these lists, Mr. Buljko, you state -- in the statement you mention that according to you -- this is at page 11 of the English and 17 of the B/C/S. According to you, the lists are about 99 per cent accurate. Why is it that you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: I say that because probably somewhere there are some overlapping names. Later on, when we got this in the electronic version, the computer came up with this. I think there were very few. This involves 15.000, 20.000, 30.000 people. I can't even remember the exact figure, but probably if you take, say, 1 per cent of that figure there must have been erroneous information that was entered at that moment, and also it may happen, say, that relatives from Blagaj would report a particular case and that relatives who were south of Mostar, that is to say, in Blagaj, said one thing whereas relatives elsewhere who did not communicate with the Blagaj relatives because there were no telephones lines that were operating then, they could not communicate. So it may happen that, say, 1 per cent was not -- well, the rest is certainly correct, except for, say, 1 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, moving on to the 24th of August, 1993. Still page 11 of the English version of your statement and 17 of the B/C/S version, where you state in the last paragraph of the English version that you were a member of the ABiH delegation negotiating with the HVO to allow the first humanitarian aid convoy to enter Mostar since the beginning of the conflict in Mostar between the HVO and the ABiH in May. And you say you made handwritten notes of the negotiation meeting. Could you take a look at Exhibit 4479.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document, well, it's my notes, actually, before it was agreed to have a cease-fire and an exchange of the dead, and it was the first time that humanitarian aid came to East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: In what capacity did you attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Well, in terms of coordinating humanitarian aid and activities, and also as an interpreter because Mr. Albert Benabou was present at these meetings, and other representatives of the international community like Mr. Jerry Hume on behalf of the UNHCR. So this was my duty to help, that after I write down what was agreed, I draft a working version of this document, that I type it out and that this working draft be approved and be sent to the Spanish Battalion that was deployed in Jablanica with a view to preparing this operation of the exchange of dead bodies and the arrival of the first convoy with humanitarian aid into East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: As you mention that -- the working draft that was to be sent to the Spanish Battalion, can you take a look at Exhibit 4480. What is that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document stemming from the previous one. I typed it out as the final document, and then it was sent on to the Spanish Battalion of UNPROFOR in Jablanica confirming the agreement of the 24th of August between the ABiH and the HVO through UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, in relation to that meeting on the 24th of August, 1993, from which you took notes that you then transformed into this draft, you mention some internationals that were present at that meeting. Who was present from the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: On behalf of the ABiH Mr. Sulejman Budakovic, as well as Mr. Alija Alikadic. So they were the main persons at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And who was present from the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO
utterances.text: On the HVO side, discussions were held through the UN civilian police, Mr. Benabou. I think that at that moment it was Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Witness, perhaps I can refer you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
